title: Week 4 · Chapter 4: Intermediate SQL
summary: The supplied Week 4 deck covers explicit joins, outer joins, views, transactions, integrity constraints, indexes, and SQL authorization. The reader keeps all 91 source pages and highlights only the high-yield distinctions.
objectives: Choose NATURAL JOIN, JOIN ... USING, or JOIN ... ON from the intended matching rule
Predict which tuples survive inner and outer joins, including MySQL's FULL OUTER JOIN workaround
Explain view updateability, transaction boundaries, and MySQL autocommit
Apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, foreign-key, and cascading-action semantics
Distinguish physical indexes from logical constraints and use GRANT/REVOKE/roles correctly

sections.title: 1. Joins: state the relationship explicitly
sections.body: A join starts from candidate tuple pairs and keeps the pairs justified by a matching rule. NATURAL JOIN uses every same-named attribute, USING names the equality columns, and ON accepts a general predicate. Use an outer join when unmatched tuples must remain visible.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Join questions expose missing predicates, accidental natural-join matches, and the difference between preserving and discarding unmatched tuples.

sections.title: 2. Views: reusable interfaces over queries
sections.body: A view gives a relation-shaped interface over a query. It can hide columns or rows, and one view can be defined from another. A view update is allowed only when the DBMS can map it unambiguously to base-table changes; a materialized view additionally stores a result that must be refreshed.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: View questions test whether you can separate a logical query interface, stored result, and legal update mapping.

sections.title: 3. Transactions: commit the unit or undo it
sections.body: A transaction groups statements into one logical unit. In MySQL, autocommit is enabled by default; START TRANSACTION keeps the unit open until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Constraint failures must be reasoned about together with the transaction boundary.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The key trap is confusing statement-level autocommit with an explicit multi-statement transaction.

sections.title: 4. Integrity constraints: keep database states legal
sections.body: NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, and CHECK constrain one relation. Foreign keys constrain a relationship between relations. ON DELETE and ON UPDATE actions determine how parent changes affect referencing rows; temporarily disabling checks changes the safety boundary.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Constraint questions are compact distinction checks: single-relation rules versus foreign-key rules and default versus cascading actions.

sections.title: 5. Data types and indexes: declare and access
sections.body: SQL data types are part of the schema contract. An index is a physical access structure that can make selective retrieval cheaper, but it does not change query semantics, make values unique, or enforce a foreign-key rule.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Index questions test physical-versus-logical reasoning and whether an access path is being confused with a constraint.

sections.title: 6. Authorization: grant the smallest required privilege
sections.body: Authorization distinguishes read, data-modification, reference, and schema privileges. GRANT assigns a privilege to a user, PUBLIC, or role; REVOKE removes it. A view can narrow the interface, but access to a view does not imply unrestricted access to its base tables.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Authorization questions are syntax-and-meaning contrasts: privilege type, grant target, revoke effect, and role inheritance.

examples.title: Debug a natural join before trusting its result
steps: List every same-named attribute in the participating relations.
Mark which equalities are intended relationship keys.
Rewrite the query with JOIN ... ON or JOIN ... USING when natural join would equate an unrelated column.
examples.answer: A successful natural join can still be semantically wrong. Make the intended key equality visible before inspecting the result.

examples.title: Recover a full outer join in MySQL
steps: Write the left outer join to preserve every left-side tuple.
Write the right outer join to preserve right-only tuples.
Combine the two results with UNION after aligning the projected columns.
examples.answer: MySQL does not provide direct FULL OUTER JOIN syntax in this deck; the two outer-join results preserve both sides.

examples.title: Predict the transaction outcome
steps: Identify whether autocommit is active or an explicit transaction has started.
Mark the statement that violates the CHECK or foreign-key constraint.
Decide whether COMMIT persists the unit or ROLLBACK removes its uncommitted effects.
examples.answer: The answer depends on the transaction boundary and the configured constraint action, not just on the order of SQL text.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why can NATURAL JOIN return too few rows even when every SQL statement succeeds?
criticalQuestions.angle: Audit all same-named attributes before accepting an implicit equality.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: NATURAL JOIN equates every same-named attribute. If one shared name is unrelated to the intended relationship, valid tuple pairs are filtered out without a syntax error.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What changes when START TRANSACTION is added before two MySQL updates?
criticalQuestions.angle: Compare an explicit transaction boundary with default autocommit.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The updates remain in one open unit until COMMIT or ROLLBACK; with autocommit, each statement is committed independently unless it is explicitly enclosed in a transaction.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does an index not replace a UNIQUE or foreign-key constraint?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate physical access cost from legal database states.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: An index is an access structure used to locate tuples efficiently. UNIQUE and foreign-key constraints enforce logical integrity conditions; they answer different questions.

math.name: Theta join
math.purpose: State the predicate that selects related tuple pairs.
math.explanation: The predicate $\theta$ controls which pairs from $R$ and $S$ appear in the joined relation.

math.name: Referential-integrity condition
math.purpose: Check whether a non-null foreign key points to an existing parent key.
math.explanation: A child foreign-key value must match a referenced parent key, unless the foreign-key value is allowed to be $NULL$.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which form is safer when two relations share a column name that is not part of the intended relationship?
choices: JOIN ... ON with an explicit predicate
contrastDrills.explanation: JOIN ... ON makes the intended relationship explicit and avoids unintended equalities over other same-named columns.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming same-named attributes always represent the same fact.

contrastDrills.pair: INNER JOIN vs LEFT OUTER JOIN
contrastDrills.prompt: Which join keeps every instructor even when that instructor teaches no section?
choices: LEFT OUTER JOIN with instructor on the left
contrastDrills.explanation: A left outer join preserves every left-side tuple and fills unmatched right-side attributes with NULL.
contrastDrills.misconception: Thinking an inner join preserves entities with no matching row.

contrastDrills.pair: LEFT OUTER JOIN vs FULL OUTER JOIN
contrastDrills.prompt: Which result preserves unmatched tuples from both input relations?
contrastDrills.explanation: A full outer join preserves the unmatched tuples from both sides; MySQL implements the deck's version by combining left and right outer joins with UNION.
contrastDrills.misconception: Treating left and full outer joins as interchangeable.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which object physically stores a query result and may need refresh?
contrastDrills.explanation: A materialized view stores the result physically, trading refresh/storage work for potentially faster reads.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming CREATE VIEW always copies and stores rows.

contrastDrills.prompt: After an explicit transaction, which statement makes its uncommitted changes durable?
contrastDrills.explanation: COMMIT ends the transaction and makes its changes durable; ROLLBACK discards its uncommitted changes.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which constraint compares a tuple's values against a predicate rather than requiring a matching parent key?
contrastDrills.explanation: CHECK enforces a predicate over a tuple; a foreign key enforces a relationship to a referenced relation.
contrastDrills.misconception: Treating all integrity constraints as key relationships.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which declaration identifies the relation's chosen primary identifier and also disallows NULL?
contrastDrills.explanation: PRIMARY KEY chooses the relation's primary identifier and carries non-null uniqueness semantics; UNIQUE declares another uniqueness rule.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming every UNIQUE constraint is the primary key.

contrastDrills.prompt: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do when a parent row is deleted?
choices: Reject the parent deletion in every case
Create an index on the child
Grant DELETE to the child user
contrastDrills.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates the parent deletion to matching child rows; a restrictive action instead blocks the deletion when references remain.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming a cascade only affects the parent relation.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which object primarily changes the access path rather than the set of legal database states?
contrastDrills.explanation: An index is physical design for retrieval. Constraints define legal states and reject or transform invalid changes.
contrastDrills.misconception: Treating an index as proof that values satisfy an integrity rule.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which statement removes a previously assigned privilege?
contrastDrills.explanation: GRANT assigns privileges; REVOKE removes them from a user or role according to the authorization chain.
contrastDrills.misconception: Confusing authorization changes with schema or data changes.

contrastDrills.prompt: Why create a database role instead of granting the same privilege separately to every user?
choices: A role groups privileges for a responsibility
A role replaces every foreign key
A role forces full public access
contrastDrills.explanation: A role groups privileges so access can be assigned and maintained by responsibility rather than by repeated per-user grants.
contrastDrills.misconception: Treating a role as a relation or a data container.

contrastDrills.prompt: What does granting SELECT on a view imply about the underlying base table privileges?
choices: It automatically grants every base-table privilege
It implies no automatic grant of privileges on the underlying relations
contrastDrills.explanation: The lecture states that granting a privilege on a view does not imply granting privileges on its underlying relations.
contrastDrills.misconception: Assuming the view grant exposes the complete logical schema.
